text: Yusef Salaam, born in 1974 in New York City to Sharonne Salaam, is an American politician, motivational speaker, and activist who has served as a member of the New York City Council representing the 9th council district since 2024. A member of the Democratic Party, Salaam was one of the Central Park Five, a group of five Black and Latino teenagers—along with Korey Wise, Kevin Richardson, Antron McCray, and Raymond Santana—who were wrongly convicted in 1990 of assaulting and raping Trisha Meili, a woman jogging in Central Park on April 19, 1989, an incident committed by Matias Reyes. At the time, Salaam was 15 years old. The teenagers initially confessed but later claimed their confessions were obtained through beatings and threats by police, with Salaam stating that officers deprived them of food, drink, or sleep for over a day. His conviction was upheld by the Appellate Division in 1990 and again by the Court of Appeals of the State of New York in 1993. He was released from prison in 1997, and his conviction was vacated in 2002. In 2014, New York City settled a civil rights lawsuit brought by the Central Park Five for $41 million. While incarcerated, Salaam deepened his connection to Islam, stating that his faith helped him endure his sentence and that he found parallels between his experience and the story of Prophet Yusuf (as) in the Quran. He served as imam of a youth facility for five years, as Qadi (religious judge) for about one and a half years, and as Naib (assistant leader) before his release. After being released, Salaam worked as a construction worker in the Mitchell–Lama Housing Program, was later fired after his identity was discovered, and then worked at Weill Cornell Medicine. He has served on the board of the Innocence Project. In 2021, he considered running for the New York State Legislature but declined due to residency requirements. He moved back to New York City from Georgia in 2022. On February 4, 2023, Salaam announced his candidacy for the 9th City Council District, representing Harlem, and was endorsed by Cornel West. He won the Democratic primary on July 5, defeating assemblymembers Inez Dickens and Al Taylor, and was unopposed in the general election, succeeding councilwoman Kristin Richardson Jordan for a term ending January 1, 2026. He was re-elected in November 2025. In January 2024, his car, which had Georgia license plates and dark-tinted windows illegal in New York, was stopped in Harlem by a police officer. When the officer approached, Salaam identified himself as a city council member on city business; he was on a business call with colleagues including City Council member Sandy Nurse, who heard the interaction. The officer, upon learning Salaam’s position, cut off the interaction and walked away, saying, "Take care, sir." Salaam said the police should have given a reason for the stop, though officers are not required to do so; critics claimed he used his position to avoid a ticket. After the second 2024 presidential debate, Salaam confronted former president Donald Trump, who had previously called for Salaam to be executed, but refused to retract those statements. Salaam is a practicing Muslim with ten children, three of whom are stepchildren. In 2016, he received a Lifetime Achievement Award from President Barack Obama, and in 2021, he was awarded the Muhammad Ali Confident Muslim of the Year by the Yaqeen Institute for Islamic Research. He is featured in Ken Burns’s documentary The Central Park Five (2012), portrayed as an adult by Chris Chalk and as a child by Ethan Herisse in Ava DuVernay’s television miniseries When They See Us. In 2022, "Gate of the Exonerated" was dedicated at the northern end of Central Park in honor of Salaam and the other members of the Exonerated Five.
